mood.p: De dag begint met veel bewolking en hier en daar regen, maar vanuit het westen breekt de zon later op steeds meer plaatsen door en wordt het 22 a 23 graden. Vrijdag is het nat en waait het stevig, daarna wordt het weekend rustiger met ruimte voor de zon en zondag zo'n 23 graden. In het land overheerst nog steeds de schrik na het geweld in Overasselt, waar een 51-jarige beveiliger om het leven kwam en de gemeente Heumen vandaag beslist over sluiting van het beschoten huis. Tegelijk klinkt in Den Haag opluchting nu de coalitie de bezuinigingen op de sociale zekerheid grotendeels heeft geschrapt, al gaat de ov-staking van 9 september gewoon door. Aan de kassa blijft het pijn doen: de benzineprijs brak deze week alle records met bijna 2,67 euro per liter en de energierekening blijft onzeker door de oorlog in het Midden-Oosten. Het is een dag van harde koppen en zacht nazomerlicht, met de blik alvast op een rustiger weekend.

global.h3: US and Iran trade threats as strike toll in Iran climbs to 18
global.summary: Tehran called an American strike that hit a wedding party a war crime while Donald Trump said US forces can hit Iran again whenever they choose.
body: Iran and the United States exchanged their sharpest threats in weeks after a barrage of American missile and drone attacks on southern Iran late on 1 September. Iranian state television, citing the health ministry, put the death toll at 18 with 108 people wounded. Iranian officials say one of the strikes hit a wedding ceremony and killed several civilians including a four year old boy, and they described the attack as a war crime.

Washington denies that civilians were targeted. US officials say the strikes were aimed at Revolutionary Guard air defence, radar, maritime and mine laying sites, and Trump said American forces could strike again at any moment. France 24 journalists geolocated footage from the town and reported that the debris and video raise questions the Pentagon has not yet answered.

Tehran responded by firing missiles and drones at American bases across the Gulf, widening a conflict that has already pushed oil prices and shipping insurance sharply higher. Regional governments are urging restraint while quietly preparing for a longer confrontation.

global.h3: Kuwait intercepts Iranian missiles as Gulf bases come under fire
global.summary: Kuwait's army said it was shooting down a missile and drone attack from Iran, part of a wave of Iranian strikes on US allies across the region.
body: Kuwait's armed forces said on Thursday morning that they were intercepting an incoming missile and drone attack launched from Iran. The strikes formed part of a coordinated Iranian response to American attacks earlier in the week and also targeted sites in Jordan, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit Ali al Salem air base in Kuwait and claimed to have destroyed a command post and drone facilities there. It also said Camp Titin in Jordan came under intense ballistic missile fire. Air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain, where the US Fifth Fleet is based.

Gulf governments have spent years trying to stay out of direct confrontation between Washington and Tehran. Being drawn in as targets leaves them exposed at a moment when Strait of Hormuz shipping is already disrupted and Asian buyers are scrambling to build oil and gas storage closer to home.

global.h3: Saudi Arabia says Iranian attack on tanker killed two Filipino sailors
global.summary: The kingdom condemned the strike on the vessel Sidr, hit by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, in one of the clearest civilian shipping casualties of the war.
body: Saudi Arabia said two Filipino crew members died when the tanker Sidr was struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. Riyadh blamed Iran for the attack and condemned the targeting of commercial shipping.

The strait carries a large share of the world's seaborne crude and liquefied natural gas. Attacks on merchant vessels have pushed war risk premiums up sharply and forced some owners to reroute or pause sailings, adding to the pressure on fuel prices in Europe and Asia.

Manila has asked for guarantees for Filipino seafarers, who make up a large share of global merchant crews. Shipowners are increasingly reluctant to send crews through the strait without naval escort.

global.h3: EU and NATO vow more pressure on Russia after Leipzig drone plot
global.summary: Brussels and the alliance called the failed drone attack on Leipzig airport a new escalation after Berlin publicly blamed Russian state agencies.
body: Germany formally accused Russia of being behind an attempted attack at Leipzig Halle airport, where an explosive laden drone was found next to a Ukrainian cargo aircraft on 4 August and defused. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said intelligence showed those involved acted for Russian state agencies.

The airport is a hub for NATO's strategic airlift work, with Ukrainian operated cargo flights carrying equipment to eastern member states and to Ukraine. EU and NATO officials described the incident as a new escalation in a campaign of sabotage and hybrid attacks across Europe.

Berlin responded by closing the Russian House cultural centre in the capital and the Russian consulate in Bonn. Moscow rejects the accusation and President Vladimir Putin has claimed Germany planted evidence.

global.h3: Russia shuts Goethe-Institut branches as row with Berlin deepens
global.summary: Moscow will close German cultural centres in three cities in retaliation for Germany closing the Russian House in Berlin.
body: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said the Goethe-Institut will be closed in Moscow, Saint Petersburg and Yekaterinburg. He framed the move as an unavoidable answer to Berlin's decision to shut the Russian House cultural centre and the Russian consulate in Bonn.

The Goethe-Institut was among the last German institutions still working inside Russia after years of expulsions and bans. Lavrov said Germany could not have failed to understand that closing the Russian House would end German cultural presence in the country.

The tit for tat closures follow Berlin's accusation that Russian state agencies were behind the Leipzig airport drone plot. Both governments have now cut most remaining channels for cultural and academic contact.

global.h3: Zelensky warns airlines that Russian airspace is no longer safe
global.summary: Kyiv asked the UN aviation agency to call for a full ban on civilian flights over Russia as Ukrainian drone strikes reach deeper into the country.
body: Ukraine has formally written to the International Civil Aviation Organization urging it to warn carriers away from Russian airspace. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian drones would make the skies over Russia completely unsafe for as long as the war continues.

The warning follows a sharp increase in long range Ukrainian strikes on Russian airfields, refineries and logistics hubs. Several Russian airports have suspended operations at short notice in recent weeks, stranding domestic passengers.

Russian officials called the statement state terrorism and said Kyiv was threatening civilian aviation. Moscow has intensified its own strikes on Ukrainian cities, with two civilians reported killed in the latest wave.

global.h3: Chevron and Eni sign huge Venezuela oil deals under US supervision
global.summary: Foreign energy firms committed to major expansions in Caracas days after Venezuela agreed to hand Washington control of a fifth of its reserves.
body: Chevron, Italy's Eni and GE Vernova signed agreements worth what US Energy Secretary Chris Wright called tens of billions of dollars at a ceremony in Caracas. Wright attended alongside interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

The deals follow an arrangement under which Venezuela granted the United States control over roughly a fifth of its oil reserves. Critics have described the process as gunpoint diplomacy given the American military operation in January that removed Nicolas Maduro from power.

Wright rejected that framing and said Washington is not trying to take Venezuelan oil but to transform the relationship between the two countries. Analysts note that any meaningful production increase will require years of investment in badly degraded infrastructure.

global.h3: Maduro claims head of state immunity to get US charges dismissed
global.summary: The deposed Venezuelan leader argues a sitting foreign head of state cannot be prosecuted in an American court.
body: Lawyers for Nicolas Maduro have asked a US judge to throw out the drug trafficking indictment against him, arguing he is immune from prosecution as a foreign head of state. Maduro was seized by American forces during the military operation in Caracas in January.

Legal scholars describe the case as unprecedented. No sitting or recently removed head of state has previously been brought before a US criminal court in this way, and the immunity question could take months to resolve.

Prosecutors say Maduro forfeited any claim to immunity because he was not recognised as the legitimate leader by Washington. A ruling against him would clear the way for a trial that Venezuela's interim government has said it will not obstruct.

global.h3: EU still split over trade sanctions on Israeli settlements
global.summary: Ireland's foreign minister said the bloc should be acting collectively to uphold international law as member states remain divided.
body: European Union governments again failed to agree on trade measures targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements. Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said the bloc should be moving collectively rather than leaving individual states to act alone.

A group of member states led by Ireland, Spain and Belgium wants suspension of trade preferences for settlement products. Others, including Germany, Hungary and Italy, argue that sanctions would remove European leverage and hurt diplomatic channels.
Because trade sanctions require broad agreement, the deadlock has left the European Commission working on narrower technical steps such as labelling and customs enforcement instead.

global.h3: China keeps its support for Iran limited as US pressure grows
global.summary: Analysts say Beijing is balancing its ties with Tehran against relationships with Gulf states and its own energy security.
body: China has offered Iran diplomatic backing and continues to buy Iranian crude, but analysts say Beijing has stopped well short of the material support Tehran wants. Chinese officials have called for de escalation without committing to anything that would put Gulf trade at risk.

Beijing's relationships with Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar are commercially far larger than its dealings with Iran. Those partners are now themselves under Iranian fire, which sharply limits how far China is willing to go.

The war has already reshaped Chinese energy demand. Oil consumption fell as prices spiked, electric vehicle sales rose and carbon dioxide emissions dropped by about one percent, a shift some analysts think may prove partly permanent.

global.h3: Macron and Burnham hold first talks after Bayeux Tapestry visit
global.summary: The French president and the new British prime minister met in London, with Channel crossings high on the agenda.
body: Emmanuel Macron and Andy Burnham were due to hold their first formal talks on Thursday, a day after appearing together at the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition at the British Museum alongside King Charles III. The loan of the tapestry has been presented by both governments as a symbol of repaired relations.

Small boat crossings in the Channel remain the most difficult item between them. A BBC investigation this week found that smuggling gangs are switching to oversized dinghies because a crackdown on supply has left them short of ordinary boats, forcing once rival groups to cooperate.

Defence cooperation, European security funding and post Brexit trade friction are also on the agenda. Burnham has signalled he wants a closer working relationship with Paris than his predecessors managed.

global.h3: EU budget talks reach Dublin with frugals and cohesion camp stuck
global.summary: Ministers meeting in Ireland must break a deadlock over the size of the bloc's next seven year spending plan.
body: EU ministers gathered in Dublin for an informal General Affairs Council dominated by the next multiannual financial framework, the spending plan covering 2028 to 2034. The Irish presidency prepared a document intended to bridge positions that have been frozen since June.

Frugal contributors including Germany, the Netherlands and the Nordic states want a budget far smaller than the figure of about 1.73 trillion euros put forward under the Cypriot presidency. The friends of cohesion group, which includes Spain and Italy, wants to protect farm subsidies and payments to poorer regions.
The framework has to be agreed unanimously by the end of 2027. With general elections due next year in almost a third of member states, negotiators want the outline settled before Christmas.

global.h3: US tariffs cast a shadow over the unsigned India trade deal
global.summary: Punitive American measures risk sinking a bilateral agreement before it is even signed, analysts warn.
body: Negotiators in New Delhi and Washington have spent months building a bilateral trade agreement meant to deepen economic ties. That promise is now undercut by punitive American tariffs that hit Indian exports across several sectors.

Indian officials say the measures make it politically difficult to sign an agreement that would require concessions on agriculture and data rules. Business groups on both sides have urged Washington to pause the tariffs while talks continue.
The dispute sits alongside broader friction over India's continued purchases of discounted Russian and Iranian crude, which Washington has repeatedly criticised.

global.h3: UN warns of supersized El Nino as countries brace for impact
global.summary: The World Meteorological Organization says the event could be the strongest in more than 70 years and last into February 2027.
body: The World Meteorological Organization has issued an unusually strong warning about the El Nino now developing in the Pacific, saying it could be the most powerful in more than seventy years. Forecasters put the likelihood of it persisting into February 2027 at close to certainty.

Secretary General Celeste Saulo said the agency had never mounted such a large mobilisation in its fifty year history and warned that the event could deliver a massive blow to communities and economies. National meteorological services across several continents have aligned behind the same outlook.

Expected effects include drought in southern Africa, Australia and parts of Southeast Asia, heavy rainfall along the Pacific coast of South America and disrupted monsoon patterns. A train of Pacific cyclones including hurricanes Lowell and Karina is already being linked to the unusually warm ocean.

global.h3: Nepal flood toll passes 1,000 as tunnel search grinds on
global.summary: Rescue crews in Rasuwa are digging and blasting to reach trapped workers while thousands remain missing across the border region.
body: The death toll from the flooding that struck Nepal and neighbouring Tibet has passed one thousand, with more than four thousand people still listed as missing. Several hundred of the missing are foreign nationals.

Al Jazeera reporters given access to the rescue operation in Rasuwa described crews digging and blasting through debris to reach workers trapped in a hydropower tunnel. Blocked highways remain the single biggest obstacle, with roads passable only as far as Nuwakot in places.

Authorities have not yet moved to the second phase of relief, which would combine humanitarian assistance with road reopening, because of the terrain and a shortage of equipment. Analysts warn that the closure of the China Nepal trade corridor will damage the local economy for years.

global.h3: Floodwaters sweep cars away as torrential rain hits eastern China
global.summary: Severe flooding rushed through streets in several eastern provinces, carrying vehicles with it.
body: Torrential rain triggered severe flooding across parts of eastern China, with footage showing water rushing down city streets and sweeping away parked cars. Emergency services carried out rescues in several districts.

The rainfall follows an already difficult summer for flood control along the Yangtze basin. Local governments have issued warnings for further downpours and have moved residents from low lying neighbourhoods.
Meteorologists link the intensity of the rainfall to unusually warm sea surface temperatures, the same conditions driving the El Nino event the UN warned about this week.

global.h3: Storm floods Toronto and cuts power to tens of thousands
global.summary: A violent thunderstorm brought hail, flooding and flight cancellations across southern Ontario.
body: A powerful storm system swept across the Greater Toronto Area on Wednesday, bringing torrential rain, large hail and a tornado risk. At the peak about 65,000 customers were without electricity, and roughly 45,000 were still cut off on Thursday morning.

The Don Valley Parkway was closed in both directions by floodwater and subway service was suspended on part of one main line during the afternoon rush. Pearson airport reported numerous delays and cancellations and urged travellers to check with airlines.
Rogers Stadium, a 50,000 capacity venue in the north of the city, sustained what its operator called significant damage. The Canadian National Exhibition closed early for the day.

global.h3: Study finds nearly half the world's farmers poisoned by pesticides
global.summary: Research commissioned by Pesticide Action Network estimates more than 400 million cases of acute poisoning every year.
body: A study published in Frontiers in Public Health estimates that between 402 and 433 million cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning occur among farmers and farm workers each year. That is close to half of the global agricultural workforce.
The researchers, working with publicly available data from 2006 to 2023, estimate that pesticide poisoning kills about 11,000 people annually. India accounts for nearly 60 percent of those deaths.

Campaigners say the figures strengthen the case for banning highly hazardous compounds that remain legal in many producing countries but are restricted in Europe. Industry groups dispute the methodology and point to gaps in reporting.

global.h3: China's emissions fall as war shock cuts oil use and lifts EV sales
global.summary: Analysts say the drop could mark a decarbonisation watershed if demand does not fully return.
body: Chinese carbon dioxide emissions fell by about one percent after the outbreak of the war on Iran, according to new analysis. The decline was driven by a sharp fall in oil consumption as prices spiked and by a surge in electric vehicle sales.

Analysts say the interesting question is whether demand rebounds once crude prices ease. Several argue that buyers who switched to electric vehicles during the price shock are unlikely to switch back, which would lock in part of the reduction.

China remains the world's largest emitter and its power sector still leans heavily on coal. Even so, a sustained decline in transport fuel demand would change the trajectory of global emissions faster than most models assume.

netherlands.h3: Cabinet scraps most welfare cuts in last minute budget deal
netherlands.summary: The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA reversed planned social security savings and delayed the healthcare deductible rise as it hunts for opposition votes.
body: After a weekend of talks that repeatedly overran their deadlines, coalition partners D66, VVD and CDA reached a budget agreement for next year. Leaked details show the cabinet is reversing most of the planned cuts to social security, including a 2.8 billion euro saving on the state pension that will now not go ahead.

The planned increase in the eigen risico, the compulsory healthcare excess, is being pushed back by a year. About 1.5 billion euros is being set aside to repair purchasing power, financed in part by roughly 750 million euros in extra tax on higher incomes.

Finance Minister Heinen has appealed to opposition parties to back the plans, saying the budget was written for ten parties rather than three. Opposition leaders remain sceptical, and Pro leader Jesse Klaver accused the coalition of manufacturing a crisis. The full documents are due on Prinsjesdag on 15 September.

netherlands.h3: Coalition pushes the box 3 wealth tax overhaul back to 2029
netherlands.summary: Savers, investors and property owners still do not know how they will be taxed from 2028 after another delay.
body: Plans to reform the Dutch box 3 system, which taxes savings, investments and second properties, look set to slip again. Coalition parties have argued for weeks over how to replace the current regime and now want to postpone the bill.

The delay means the rules for 2028 remain unclear, leaving households and their advisers unable to plan. Successive cabinets have promised a system based on actual returns rather than assumed ones, and successive cabinets have missed the deadline.
The Tax Administration has warned repeatedly that it needs long lead times to implement any new system. Each postponement makes an eventual start date later still.

netherlands.h3: Court again blocks the return of asylum seekers to Italy
netherlands.summary: The Hague court ruled that conditions for returnees are still inadequate despite the new EU migration pact.
body: A court in The Hague ruled that the Netherlands still may not send asylum seekers back to Italy under the Dublin rules. The judges found that living conditions for people returned to Italy remain insufficiently guaranteed.
The cabinet had argued that the new European migration pact changed the legal picture. The court disagreed, saying the pact does not by itself resolve the concrete shortcomings in Italian reception.
It is another legal setback for a government that has made faster returns central to its migration policy. Similar rulings have blocked transfers to several other member states.

netherlands.h3: Over 230 former ministers and diplomats demand tougher line on Israel
netherlands.summary: The signatories say the Dutch government is failing its own commitments to international law.
body: More than 230 former Dutch ministers, ambassadors, diplomats and senior civil servants have signed an appeal urging the cabinet to take far tougher measures against Israel. The group argues that current policy does not match the Netherlands' stated commitment to international law.
The letter lands as EU member states remain divided over trade measures targeting goods from illegal settlements. The Netherlands has so far sided with the more cautious camp in Brussels.

Signatories include figures from across the political spectrum, which makes the intervention harder for the cabinet to dismiss as partisan. Parliament is expected to debate the issue after the budget.

netherlands.h3: Dutch central bank shifts 86 tonnes of gold to London
netherlands.summary: DNB says holding more reserves in London lets it act faster in a crisis, citing increasing geopolitical unrest.
body: De Nederlandsche Bank has moved about 86 tonnes of gold out of New York and Ottawa to London between March and August. The bank said the transfer was driven by increasing geopolitical unrest and by the need to be able to act quickly in a crisis situation.

London's share of the Dutch gold reserve rose from 18.1 percent to 32.1 percent, making it the largest single storage location. New York and Ottawa now hold 18.5 percent each, down from 31.3 and 19.7 percent.

More than 27 tonnes of physical bullion was shipped from North America to Zeist and an equal quantity moved from Zeist to London, which avoided melting bars down. The rest was handled by selling in New York and buying back in London.

netherlands.h3: Petrol price hits a record 2.67 euro a litre
netherlands.summary: Experts say the new peak is unlikely to push many Dutch drivers out of their cars.
body: The recommended price for a litre of petrol reached about 2.668 euros, a new record, according to consumer collective UnitedConsumers. The rise is driven by the oil price shock from the war in the Middle East.

Analysts say demand is stubbornly insensitive to price at these levels because most driving is commuting or other trips people cannot easily drop. What changes instead is discretionary spending elsewhere in household budgets.

The same energy shock is showing up in other numbers. August inflation came in at 3.3 percent, and the Nationaal Warmtefonds has already issued more loans for home insulation and heat pumps this year than in the whole of 2025.

netherlands.h3: Student housing shortage barely shrinks despite building targets met
netherlands.summary: The national monitor puts the gap at more than 20,000 homes, only slightly below last year.
body: The shortage of student housing in the Netherlands has barely improved, according to the Landelijke Monitor Studentenhuisvesting. The gap stands at just over 20,200 homes compared with about 21,000 a year earlier, even though agreed construction targets were met.
Providers have built close to 5,000 units a year on average since 2022. Knowledge centre Kences says that pace is not enough and that more measures are needed to close the gap.

Researchers also point to a hidden shortage. Thousands of students have stopped searching altogether because they consider the market hopeless, which means the official figure understates the real problem.

netherlands.h3: Up to 1,300 building projects face a halt after inspector suspension
netherlands.summary: The association of municipalities warns that suspended quality assurance bureaus will stop work on sites across the country.
body: The Association of Netherlands Municipalities has warned that as many as 1,300 construction projects may have to be stopped after one of the largest quality assurance bureaus was suspended. Quality assurers check during design and on site whether simpler buildings such as family homes meet the legal technical requirements.

When an assurer loses its accreditation the municipality must halt construction immediately. Work can only restart once the suspension is lifted or another qualified bureau takes over the inspections.
Two bureaus appear on the suspension list of the admissions body for construction quality assurance, one in Amersfoort and one in Heerlen. A third firm in The Hague was suspended in May.

netherlands.h3: Heumen weighs closing Overasselt house as weapons are found
netherlands.summary: Police ended their search of the Gelderland village after an armed group attacked a property, killing a 51 year old security guard.
body: Riot police concluded an extensive search in and around Overasselt following Tuesday's attack, in which roughly thirty masked and partly armed men descended on a property on the Ewijkseweg before dawn. A 51 year old security guard from Wijchen was killed and two police officers were wounded.

Officers found several weapons inside the search area and more outside it. Investigators say the suspects had gathered at a warehouse in Brussels before travelling to the Netherlands, and a threatening video linked to the attack has surfaced online.

The municipality of Heumen was due to announce on Thursday whether the house will be closed. Justice Minister Van Weel called the form of the violence something the Netherlands has not seen before, describing groups of dozens of armed young men moving openly through a village.

netherlands.h3: Police and prosecutors warn of fast changing cybercrime threat
netherlands.summary: The biannual Cybercrimebeeld Nederland points to state involvement and AI as the drivers, with 2.5 million victims last year.
body: The police and the Public Prosecution Service published their biannual Cybercrimebeeld Nederland, warning that the cyber threat to the country is changing rapidly. They single out interference by states and the use of artificial intelligence by criminals as the two clearest shifts.
Around 2.5 million people in the Netherlands were victims of online crime or online fraud, deception, threats or intimidation last year. That is roughly 17 percent of everyone aged 15 and over.

Online fraud and scams were the most common category at about 10 percent, followed by hacking at 6 percent. Just over half of victims told the police or another organisation what happened, but only 15 percent filed a formal report.

netherlands.h3: Chemicals above safe limits found in Dutch swimming water
netherlands.summary: Water quality is barely improving and swimmers are not told about the chemical readings.
body: The quality of Dutch bathing water is hardly improving, according to new figures. Alongside bacteria and blue green algae, many swimming locations contain chemical substances at levels above the official norms.

Among the compounds found frequently is a pesticide used in flea collars for dogs. Swimmers receive no information about the chemical readings because the public warning system only covers bacteria and algae.
The findings come in the same week that Amsterdam switched off nineteen fountains after E. coli bacteria were detected in some of them, which can cause stomach and intestinal complaints.

netherlands.h3: AI firms buy up second hand Dutch books to train language models
netherlands.summary: Booksellers say obscure titles are being bought in bulk, scanned and then destroyed.
body: Technology companies are buying second hand Dutch language books on a large scale to train their language models. Dutch and Belgian booksellers report bulk orders for obscure titles, particularly those published before 2022.

One Canadian buyer, Zoom Books, approached the Dutch chain De Slegte with a request for 800,000 Dutch language books. Sellers suspect the volumes are cut apart and scanned, with the physical copies destroyed afterwards.

Authors say they never gave permission for their work to be used this way. The practice is already the subject of litigation abroad, and Sony Music and Warner Music this week sued Anthropic in the United States over the use of song lyrics in training data.

netherlands.h3: Researchers find little proven help for girls drawn into crime
netherlands.summary: A new study says almost no treatment programmes are demonstrably effective for girls and young women in the justice system.
body: There is very little help with demonstrable results for girls and young women who end up in crime, according to researchers. Existing programmes were largely designed around boys and young men and are simply applied to girls without adaptation.

The study concludes that more treatments aimed specifically at this group are needed. The authors point to differences in how girls enter criminal networks, often through coercion or relationships rather than peer groups.
The number of girls appearing in Dutch criminal cases has risen in recent years, including in drug related and violent offences. Youth care providers say they lack the tools to respond.
